Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

On this page the scalar field is the field $\mathbb R$ of real numbers: $X$, $Y$
and $Z$ always denote real Banach spaces ([[def-banach-space]]) and $U
\subseteq X$ always denotes an open subset of $X$, in the metric topology of the
norm ([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $f : U \to Y$ be a map and let $x \in U$. For a bounded linear operator
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) write

$$r(h) := f(x+h) - f(x) - Th \qquad (h \in X,\ x+h \in U).$$

Then $f$ is **Fréchet differentiable at $x$** when there is
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ with

$$\lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \ne 0}} \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Th\|}{\|h\|} = 0 ,$$

the limit being taken over those $h$ with $x + h \in U$. Such an operator $T$ is
a **Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$**, written $T = Df(x)$, and $\|T\|$ is its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). When $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at
every point of $U$, $f$ is **differentiable on $U$** and the **derivative** is
the map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Banach spaces and let $U \subseteq X$ be open. All
derivatives below are Fréchet derivatives
([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]), and all continuity is with
respect to the norm metrics ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

* $f : U \to Y$ is of **class $C^0$** when $f$ is continuous on $U$.
* $f$ is of **class $C^1$** when $f$ is differentiable on $U$ and its derivative
  map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$ is continuous for the operator norm on
  $\mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-operator-norm]],
  [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]).
* For $k \ge 1$ define the spaces of iterated derivative values by
  $$\mathcal B_0 := Y, \qquad \mathcal B_{k} := \mathcal B(X,\mathcal B_{k-1}).$$
  Each $\mathcal B_k$ is a real Banach space for the operator norm, by induction
  on $k$ from [[thm-bounded-operator-space-is-banach]]. Then $f$ is of **class
  $C^{k}$** when $f$ is of class $C^{k-1}$, the map
  $D^{k-1}f : U \to \mathcal B_{k-1}$ is differentiable on $U$, where
  $D^0f := f$, and the **$k$-th derivative**
  $D^k f : U \to \mathcal B_k$ is continuous for the operator norm on
  $\mathcal B_k$. We write $D^kf(x)$ for the value at $x$.
* $f$ is of **class $C^\infty$** when $f$ is of class $C^k$ for every $k \ge 0$.

For open sets $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq Y$, a map $f : U \to V$ is a
**$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when it is a bijection, $f$ is of class $C^k$ and
$f^{-1} : V \to U$ is of class $C^k$; likewise with $C^\infty$ in place of
$C^k$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $X$ be a Banach space, $a<b$, and let $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ in the sense of [[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]. If there is $C\ge0$ with $\|\varphi'(s)\| \le C$ for all $s\in(a,b)$, then $\|\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\| \le C(b-a)$. In particular, if $\varphi$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $\varphi'=0$ there, then $\varphi$ is constant.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$
carry the subspace metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Under countable choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]),
   if $(A,d_A)$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]), then $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). No completeness hypothesis on $X$ is needed.
2. **In ZF, without a choice axiom**, if $(X,d)$ is complete and $A$ is closed
   in $(X,d)$, then $(A,d_A)$ is complete.

Consequently, under countable choice, a subspace of a complete metric space is
complete if and only if it is closed.

The following form of the first direction is also choice-free: a complete
subspace contains the ambient limit of every convergent sequence of its
points. Hence it is closed whenever every point of its ambient closure is
already known to be the limit of a sequence from that subspace. This last
condition is pointwise existence, not a chosen family of sequences.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

derivations.claim: Uniform contraction bound. Define $T_\epsilon(x):=x-L^{-1}F(x,\epsilon)$ wherever $(x,\epsilon)\in U$. Then $D_xT_0(0)=I-L^{-1}L=0$. By continuity of $D_xF$, choose $\rho>0$, $\epsilon_1>0$, and $q\in(0,1)$ such that the closed product $\overline B_X(0,\rho)\times[-\epsilon_1,\epsilon_1]$ lies in $U$ and $\|D_xT_\epsilon(x)\|\leq q$ there. For fixed $\epsilon$ and $x,y$ in the ball, the curve $s\mapsto T_\epsilon(y+s(x-y))$ is continuous and differentiable with derivative norm at most $q\|x-y\|$; [F5] therefore gives $\|T_\epsilon(x)-T_\epsilon(y)\|\leq q\|x-y\|$.

Fixed points and local uniqueness. Since $T_0(0)=0$, continuity of $F$ allows $\epsilon_0\in(0,\epsilon_1]$ such that $\|T_\epsilon(0)\|<(1-q)\rho$ for $|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$. Step 1.1 then gives $\|T_\epsilon(x)\|\leq q\rho+\|T_\epsilon(0)\|<\rho$ whenever $\|x\|\leq\rho$, so $T_\epsilon$ maps the nonempty closed ball $\overline B_X(0,\rho)$ into itself and its fixed point lies in the open ball. It is complete by [F1] and [F6], and is a contraction by step 1.1. By [F3] it has exactly one fixed point $x(\epsilon)$, and $T_\epsilon(x)=x$ is equivalent to $F(x,\epsilon)=0$ because $L^{-1}$ is injective. Thus the zero set in the product neighborhood is the graph of $x$, and $x(0)=0$.

Invertibility of nearby partial derivatives. Let $B(X)$ be the bounded linear operators on $X$, with the norm of [F7]. It is complete in the operator norm: an operator-norm Cauchy sequence converges pointwise to a linear map, the uniform norm bounds make that limit bounded, and the same Cauchy estimate gives convergence in operator norm. Shrinking the product neighborhood if necessary, continuity of $D_xF$ gives $\|L^{-1}D_xF(x,\epsilon)-I\|\leq q<1$. Put $E=L^{-1}D_xF-I$. The series $\sum_{j=0}^\infty(-E)^j$ converges in $B(X)$ because $\sum_j\|E\|^j<\infty$, and its finite partial sums multiplied on either side by $I+E$ converge to $I$; thus $D_xF(x,\epsilon)$ is invertible. The inverse is continuous, since $A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}$ for invertible nearby operators with uniformly bounded inverses.

Continuity and a local Lipschitz bound. For $\epsilon,\eta$ in a smaller interval, the fixed-point equations and step 1.1 yield $\|x(\epsilon)-x(\eta)\|\leq(1-q)^{-1}\|T_\epsilon(x(\eta))-T_\eta(x(\eta))\|$. The derivative $D_\epsilon F$ is bounded on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(0,0)$, since it is continuous there; applying [F5] to the parameter segment bounds the right-hand side by $C|\epsilon-\eta|$. Hence $x$ is locally Lipschitz, in particular continuous.

Differentiation of the branch. Write $\delta x=x(\epsilon+h)-x(\epsilon)$. Step 3.1 gives $\|\delta x\|=O(|h|)$. Fréchet differentiability at $(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)$ yields $0=D_xF(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)\delta x+D_\epsilon F(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)h+o(\|\delta x\|+|h|)$. Divide by $h\ne0$; the remainder divided by $|h|$ tends to zero because $\|\delta x\|=O(|h|)$. Multiplying by the bounded inverse from step 2.2 gives $\delta x/h\to-D_xF(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)^{-1}D_\epsilon F(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)$. This proves differentiability and the displayed formula. The formula is continuous in $\epsilon$ because $x$, $DF$, and the nearby operator inverse are continuous. Therefore $x$ is $C^1$ on a possibly smaller interval, which proves the statement.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty, bounded, connected open set with smooth boundary, meaning each boundary point has Euclidean coordinates in which $\Omega$ is one side of a smooth graph. Use Euclidean coordinates $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $\delta=\sum_{i=1}^3dx^i\otimes dx^i$, write $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$, and set $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i^2$. A multi-index is $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$; write $|\beta|=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3$ and $D^\beta=\partial_1^{\beta_1}\partial_2^{\beta_2}\partial_3^{\beta_3}$. Fix $0<\alpha<1$, a real function $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $S\geq0$, and a real dimensionless parameter $\varepsilon$. For a real function $g$ on $\overline\Omega$, define

$$[g]_{0,\alpha}:=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|g(x)-g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha},\qquad \|g\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{\overline\Omega}|g|+[g]_{0,\alpha},$$

and let $C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ consist of the continuous functions with finite displayed norm. Define $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ to consist of functions whose derivatives through order $2$ on $\Omega$ extend continuously to $\overline\Omega$ and whose norm

$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}:=\sum_{|\beta|\leq2}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta u|+\sum_{|\beta|=2}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha}$$

is finite, where $\beta$ is a multi-index. Write $X:=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$, with its inherited norm, and $Y:=C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The bounded-domain charged conformal problem is to find $u\in X$ such that $\psi:=1+u>0$ on $\overline\Omega$ and

$$-8\Delta\psi=2\varepsilon^2 S\psi^{-3}\quad\hbox{in }\Omega,\qquad \psi|_{\partial\Omega}=1.$$

In the conformal-seed specialization $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, and $\Lambda=0$ (so $h=\psi^4\delta$ and $K=0$), the initial data are time-symmetric, meaning their second fundamental form is $K=0$. The scalar equation is the Hamiltonian constraint from the conformal electrovacuum transformation when $S=|\bar E_0|_\delta^2+|\bar B_0|_\delta^2$. Here $\bar E_0,\bar B_0:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are independently prescribed contravariant Euclidean vector fields, each the restriction of a smooth map on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and divergence-free means $\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$ on $\Omega$ in these Cartesian coordinates. The actual barred seed fields are $\bar E=\varepsilon\bar E_0$ and $\bar B=\varepsilon\bar B_0$. In geometric length coordinates, $\psi,\varepsilon$ are dimensionless, $\bar E_0,\bar B_0$ have units of inverse length, and $S$ has units of inverse length squared. This is a specialization with prescribed fields; the general problem allows any nonnegative $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, a momentum constraint, or an asymptotically Euclidean or puncture solution.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain and choose $R>0$ with $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^3$. Write $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of the compactly supported smooth functions. Then $\|v\|_{L^2}\le2R\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. A function $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ represents an element of $H^1_0(\Omega)$ if and only if $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ and $0<\alpha<1$ there is $C=C(\Omega,\alpha)$ such that every $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with zero boundary restriction satisfies

$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|\Delta u\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}+\|u\|_{C^0(\overline\Omega)}\bigr).$$

The Hölder norms are the full derivative-supremum plus top-seminorm norms. The constant does not depend on higher derivatives of $u$; this is an a priori estimate, in particular for smooth approximants, not an assumed weak-to-classical existence theorem.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, nonempty and open. If $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $\Delta u\ge0$, then
$$\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u.$$
No connectedness or boundary smoothness is required.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice (for the Sobolev embedding and the trace
characterisation) and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^\infty$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and suppose $a^{ij},b^i,c,f$ extend to $C^\infty$ functions on a
neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak
solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^m(\Omega)$ for every $m$; $u$ agrees almost everywhere with a
function $\widetilde u\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$ satisfying $Lu=f$
pointwise in $\Omega$, and $\widetilde u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$. The boundary
values are those of the continuous representative, consistent with the trace
characterisation of [[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]]; the
statement asserts no pointwise boundary condition for the Sobolev class
itself.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, $0<\alpha<1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty. Then $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with the norm of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] is a Banach space over $\mathbb K$: every Cauchy sequence in $\|\cdot\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ converges in that norm to a limit whose $k$-th partial derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder on $\Omega$. If in addition $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain with nonempty boundary, then the subspace
$$X_0:=\{u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega): u\text{ extends continuously to }\bar\Omega\text{ with }u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$$
is closed in $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega)$ and hence is a Banach space. For every bounded open nonempty $\Omega$, the boundary-extension class $C^{k,\alpha}(\bar\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is also a closed subspace of $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and hence a Banach space, as is its zero-boundary subspace. Completeness here is for the full finite Hölder norm. A boundary Hölder seminorm alone does not define a norm on this function space, since it vanishes on nonzero constant functions.

derivations.claim: Weak construction. Put $H=H^1_0(\Omega)$, $a(v,w)=\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\nabla w$, and $\ell_f(w)=\frac18\int_\Omega f w$. Boundedness of $\Omega$ gives $f\in L^2$. By [F3] and the locally proved [F4], $|\ell_f(w)|\le C_P\|f\|_2\|w\|_{H^1}/8$. Also $|a(v,w)|\le\|v\|_{H^1}\|w\|_{H^1}$ and $\|w\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+C_P^2)a(w,w)$. By [F2] and [F5] there is exactly one $u_f\in H$ with $a(u_f,w)=\ell_f(w)$ for every $w\in H$; [F8] identifies its equation as $-\Delta u_f=f/8$. When $f=0$ this solution is zero.

Smooth approximation without assuming density in the full Hölder norm. Set $F=f/8$. For real data extend $F$ from $\overline\Omega$ by $\inf_{z\in\overline\Omega}(F(z)+[F]_\alpha|x-z|^\alpha)$, clamp to $[-\|F\|_\infty,\|F\|_\infty]$, and multiply by a fixed smooth cutoff equal to one near $\overline\Omega$. The Hölder inequality for $F$ proves equality on the closure, and $(a+b)^\alpha\le a^\alpha+b^\alpha$ proves the global Hölder bound. Convolve this compact extension with mollifiers of radii tending to zero. By [F10] the resulting $F_m$ are smooth on a neighborhood of the closure; direct averaging gives $\sup_m\|F_m\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le C\|F\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$ and $F_m\to F$ uniformly. Convergence in the full $C^{0,\alpha}$ norm is neither needed nor asserted. Apply step 1.1 with datum $8F_m$ to obtain $u_m\in H^1_0$ solving $-\Delta u_m=F_m$. By [F9] these have smooth representatives up to the boundary, and [F4] identifies their zero classical boundary values.

Uniform local-to-global Schauder control. Choose $B_R(x_0)$ containing $\overline\Omega$, set $M_m=\|F_m\|_\infty$ and $q_m(x)=M_m(R^2-|x-x_0|^2)/6$. Then $q_m\ge0$, $\Delta q_m=-M_m$, and $\Delta(u_m-q_m)=M_m-F_m\ge0$, $\Delta(-u_m-q_m)=M_m+F_m\ge0$. Their boundary values are $-q_m\le0$, so [F7] gives $|u_m|\le q_m$. Apply the locally proved finite-chart estimate [F6] to $u_m$. It follows that $\|u_m\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le C(\|F_m\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u_m\|_\infty)\le C'\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}/8$, uniformly in $m$. No quoted global Schauder theorem or boundary regularity theorem has supplied this estimate.

Closing the approximation and identifying the weak solution. Apply [F11] to $(u_m,Du_m,D^2u_m)$ on the compact closure. Uniform bounds and equicontinuity follow from step 3.1 and the finite smooth atlas, so a subsequence converges uniformly to $(u,G,H)$. On each interior ball the fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments gives $Du=G$ and $DG=H$. These fields are continuous on the closure, and passing to every Hessian difference quotient gives $[D^2u]_\alpha\le\liminf_m[D^2u_m]_\alpha$. Thus $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with the uniform estimate. Uniform convergence of $F_m$ and $D^2u_m$ gives $-\Delta u=F$, while $u=0$ on the boundary. The local closure result [F4] gives $u\in H^1_0$. Integrating against compactly supported smooth tests and passing to their $H^1$ closure extends the weak identity to every $H^1_0$ test. Uniqueness in step 1.1 identifies $u=u_f$. Therefore $Au_f=f$ for $A=-8\Delta$, with $\|u_f\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le C\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$.

Boundedness and uniqueness. The full norm gives $\|\Delta w\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le C\|w\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}$, so $A:X\to Y$ is bounded and linear. If $Aw=0$, then $\Delta w=0$ and $w=0$ on the boundary. Apply [F7] to $w$ and $-w$ to obtain $w=0$. Thus step 4.1 gives a bounded linear inverse. Since $A=8(-\Delta)$, $-\Delta$ is also a bounded linear isomorphism.

Uniform estimates for an explicit continuation family. To record the continuation step, put $A_t=-8\Delta+tI:X\to Y$, $0\le t\le1$. Choose $q=(R^2-|x-x_0|^2)/24>0$ on the closure, so $A_tq=2+tq\ge2$. At an interior positive maximum of $w$, $-8\Delta w+tw\ge0$. Applying this to $u-\|A_tu\|_\infty q$ and its negative counterpart excludes a positive maximum because their $A_t$ images are strictly negative when that norm is nonzero; for zero norm use an arbitrarily small positive multiple of $q$ and pass to zero. Thus $\|u\|_\infty\le C\|A_tu\|_\infty$ uniformly in $t$. For every $\eta>0$, $\|u\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\le\eta\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}+C_\eta\|u\|_\infty$: sufficiently close points in one boundary chart or interior ball can be joined inside that patch by a path of length at most $C|x-y|$, giving $|u(x)-u(y)|\le C\|Du\|_\infty|x-y|$; split pairs at a fixed small distance $\delta$ and choose $C\delta^{1-\alpha}\le\eta$. Use [F6] with $\Delta u=(tu-A_tu)/8$, absorb the small multiple, and use the supremum bound to obtain $\|u\|_X\le M\|A_tu\|_Y$ uniformly for $t\in[0,1]$.

Open and closed continuation. By [F12], $X,Y$ are Banach, and step 5.1 supplies the bijective base $A_0$. If $A_s$ is bijective, then for $|t-s|\,\|A_s^{-1}I\|<1$ the convergent geometric operator series in $-(t-s)A_s^{-1}I$ inverts $I+(t-s)A_s^{-1}I$, so $A_t$ is bijective. For closedness let $t_j\to t$ with $A_{t_j}$ bijective. Given $f\in Y$, put $v_j=A_{t_j}^{-1}f$. The uniform estimate of step 6.1 gives $\|v_j\|_X\le M\|f\|_Y$ and $\|v_j-v_k\|_X\le M|t_j-t_k|\,\|v_k\|_Y\le C M^2|t_j-t_k|\,\|f\|_Y$. Hence $v_j$ converges in $X$ and its limit solves $A_tv=f$. Injectivity follows from the same uniform estimate. The solvability set is nonempty, open and closed in $[0,1]$, so equals that interval. This continuation is based on the locally constructed Laplace inverse, not an assumed Schauder solvability result.

Steps 1.1--5.1 prove precisely the isomorphisms and inverse bound in the Statement. Steps 6.1--7.1 give the explicit continuation argument with uniformly controlled norms. The boundary estimate used in closing the weak construction is locally proved from trace/density, Newtonian Hölder cancellation, normal-jet lifting, reflection, finite flattened charts and coefficient absorption. No infinite-domain or stronger boundary-data assertion is made.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty, bounded, connected open set with smooth boundary, meaning each boundary point has Euclidean coordinates in which $\Omega$ is one side of a smooth graph. Use Euclidean coordinates $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $\delta=\sum_{i=1}^3dx^i\otimes dx^i$, write $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$, and set $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i^2$. A multi-index is $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$; write $|\beta|=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3$ and $D^\beta=\partial_1^{\beta_1}\partial_2^{\beta_2}\partial_3^{\beta_3}$. Fix $0<\alpha<1$, a real function $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $S\geq0$, and a real dimensionless parameter $\varepsilon$. For a real function $g$ on $\overline\Omega$, define

$$[g]_{0,\alpha}:=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|g(x)-g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha},\qquad \|g\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{\overline\Omega}|g|+[g]_{0,\alpha},$$

and let $C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ consist of the continuous functions with finite displayed norm. Define $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ to consist of functions whose derivatives through order $2$ on $\Omega$ extend continuously to $\overline\Omega$ and whose norm

$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}:=\sum_{|\beta|\leq2}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta u|+\sum_{|\beta|=2}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha}$$

is finite, where $\beta$ is a multi-index. Write $X:=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$, with its inherited norm, and $Y:=C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The bounded-domain charged conformal problem is to find $u\in X$ such that $\psi:=1+u>0$ on $\overline\Omega$ and

$$-8\Delta\psi=2\varepsilon^2 S\psi^{-3}\quad\hbox{in }\Omega,\qquad \psi|_{\partial\Omega}=1.$$

In the conformal-seed specialization $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, and $\Lambda=0$ (so $h=\psi^4\delta$ and $K=0$), the initial data are time-symmetric, meaning their second fundamental form is $K=0$. The scalar equation is the Hamiltonian constraint from the conformal electrovacuum transformation when $S=|\bar E_0|_\delta^2+|\bar B_0|_\delta^2$. Here $\bar E_0,\bar B_0:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are independently prescribed contravariant Euclidean vector fields, each the restriction of a smooth map on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and divergence-free means $\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$ on $\Omega$ in these Cartesian coordinates. The actual barred seed fields are $\bar E=\varepsilon\bar E_0$ and $\bar B=\varepsilon\bar B_0$. In geometric length coordinates, $\psi,\varepsilon$ are dimensionless, $\bar E_0,\bar B_0$ have units of inverse length, and $S$ has units of inverse length squared. This is a specialization with prescribed fields; the general problem allows any nonnegative $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, a momentum constraint, or an asymptotically Euclidean or puncture solution.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, $0<\alpha<1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty. Then $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with the norm of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] is a Banach space over $\mathbb K$: every Cauchy sequence in $\|\cdot\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ converges in that norm to a limit whose $k$-th partial derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder on $\Omega$. If in addition $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain with nonempty boundary, then the subspace
$$X_0:=\{u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega): u\text{ extends continuously to }\bar\Omega\text{ with }u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$$
is closed in $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega)$ and hence is a Banach space. For every bounded open nonempty $\Omega$, the boundary-extension class $C^{k,\alpha}(\bar\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is also a closed subspace of $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and hence a Banach space, as is its zero-boundary subspace. Completeness here is for the full finite Hölder norm. A boundary Hölder seminorm alone does not define a norm on this function space, since it vanishes on nonzero constant functions.

On this page the scalar field is the field $\mathbb R$ of real numbers: $X$, $Y$
and $Z$ always denote real Banach spaces ([[def-banach-space]]) and $U
\subseteq X$ always denotes an open subset of $X$, in the metric topology of the
norm ([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $f : U \to Y$ be a map and let $x \in U$. For a bounded linear operator
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) write

$$r(h) := f(x+h) - f(x) - Th \qquad (h \in X,\ x+h \in U).$$

Then $f$ is **Fréchet differentiable at $x$** when there is
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ with

$$\lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \ne 0}} \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Th\|}{\|h\|} = 0 ,$$

the limit being taken over those $h$ with $x + h \in U$. Such an operator $T$ is
a **Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$**, written $T = Df(x)$, and $\|T\|$ is its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). When $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at
every point of $U$, $f$ is **differentiable on $U$** and the **derivative** is
the map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Banach spaces and let $U \subseteq X$ be open. All
derivatives below are Fréchet derivatives
([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]), and all continuity is with
respect to the norm metrics ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

* $f : U \to Y$ is of **class $C^0$** when $f$ is continuous on $U$.
* $f$ is of **class $C^1$** when $f$ is differentiable on $U$ and its derivative
  map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$ is continuous for the operator norm on
  $\mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-operator-norm]],
  [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]).
* For $k \ge 1$ define the spaces of iterated derivative values by
  $$\mathcal B_0 := Y, \qquad \mathcal B_{k} := \mathcal B(X,\mathcal B_{k-1}).$$
  Each $\mathcal B_k$ is a real Banach space for the operator norm, by induction
  on $k$ from [[thm-bounded-operator-space-is-banach]]. Then $f$ is of **class
  $C^{k}$** when $f$ is of class $C^{k-1}$, the map
  $D^{k-1}f : U \to \mathcal B_{k-1}$ is differentiable on $U$, where
  $D^0f := f$, and the **$k$-th derivative**
  $D^k f : U \to \mathcal B_k$ is continuous for the operator norm on
  $\mathcal B_k$. We write $D^kf(x)$ for the value at $x$.
* $f$ is of **class $C^\infty$** when $f$ is of class $C^k$ for every $k \ge 0$.

For open sets $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq Y$, a map $f : U \to V$ is a
**$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when it is a bijection, $f$ is of class $C^k$ and
$f^{-1} : V \to U$ is of class $C^k$; likewise with $C^\infty$ in place of
$C^k$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Bounded inclusion. Compactness of $\overline\Omega$ and the smooth boundary give a finite cover by interior balls and flattened boundary boxes whose smaller concentric patches still cover $\overline\Omega$. In an interior patch, sufficiently close points can be joined by a segment; in a boundary patch, flattening identifies the domain locally with one side of a graph, and the inverse graph map and its inverse are Lipschitz on the smaller box. Therefore there are $\delta,C_0>0$ such that any $x,y\in\overline\Omega$ with $|x-y|<\delta$ can be joined in $\overline\Omega$ by a curve of length at most $C_0|x-y|$: take a Lebesgue number for the finite smaller-patch cover and pull back the straight segment in the corresponding ball or half-box. For boundary endpoints, approximate both endpoints by interior points in the same patch and pass to the limit using the continuous extensions of $u$ and its first derivatives. The fundamental theorem of calculus along these curves gives $|u(x)-u(y)|\leq C_0\|\nabla u\|_\infty|x-y|$ for such pairs. For $|x-y|\geq\delta$, the quotient is at most $2\delta^{-\alpha}\|u\|_\infty$. Consequently $[u]_{0,\alpha}\leq C(\|u\|_\infty+\|\nabla u\|_\infty)$, so $\|u\|_Y\leq C\|u\|_X$.

The Hölder norm is an algebra norm. For $f,g\in Y$, the identity $f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)=f(x)(g(x)-g(y))+g(y)(f(x)-f(y))$ gives $[fg]_{0,\alpha}\leq\|f\|_\infty[g]_{0,\alpha}+\|g\|_\infty[f]_{0,\alpha}$, hence $\|fg\|_Y\leq\|f\|_Y\|g\|_Y$. By [F4], the positive minimum $m=\min_{\overline\Omega}(1+u)$ exists; if $\|h\|_Y<m/2$, then $1+u+h\geq m/2>0$, so $\mathcal U$ is open.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty, bounded, connected open set with smooth boundary, meaning each boundary point has Euclidean coordinates in which $\Omega$ is one side of a smooth graph. Use Euclidean coordinates $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$, let $\delta=\sum_{i=1}^3dx^i\otimes dx^i$, write $\partial_i=\partial/\partial x^i$, and set $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i^2$. A multi-index is $\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$; write $|\beta|=\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3$ and $D^\beta=\partial_1^{\beta_1}\partial_2^{\beta_2}\partial_3^{\beta_3}$. Fix $0<\alpha<1$, a real function $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $S\geq0$, and a real dimensionless parameter $\varepsilon$. For a real function $g$ on $\overline\Omega$, define

$$[g]_{0,\alpha}:=\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|g(x)-g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha},\qquad \|g\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}:=\sup_{\overline\Omega}|g|+[g]_{0,\alpha},$$

and let $C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ consist of the continuous functions with finite displayed norm. Define $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ to consist of functions whose derivatives through order $2$ on $\Omega$ extend continuously to $\overline\Omega$ and whose norm

$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}:=\sum_{|\beta|\leq2}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta u|+\sum_{|\beta|=2}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha}$$

is finite, where $\beta$ is a multi-index. Write $X:=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$, with its inherited norm, and $Y:=C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The bounded-domain charged conformal problem is to find $u\in X$ such that $\psi:=1+u>0$ on $\overline\Omega$ and

$$-8\Delta\psi=2\varepsilon^2 S\psi^{-3}\quad\hbox{in }\Omega,\qquad \psi|_{\partial\Omega}=1.$$

In the conformal-seed specialization $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, and $\Lambda=0$ (so $h=\psi^4\delta$ and $K=0$), the initial data are time-symmetric, meaning their second fundamental form is $K=0$. The scalar equation is the Hamiltonian constraint from the conformal electrovacuum transformation when $S=|\bar E_0|_\delta^2+|\bar B_0|_\delta^2$. Here $\bar E_0,\bar B_0:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ are independently prescribed contravariant Euclidean vector fields, each the restriction of a smooth map on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and divergence-free means $\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$ on $\Omega$ in these Cartesian coordinates. The actual barred seed fields are $\bar E=\varepsilon\bar E_0$ and $\bar B=\varepsilon\bar B_0$. In geometric length coordinates, $\psi,\varepsilon$ are dimensionless, $\bar E_0,\bar B_0$ have units of inverse length, and $S$ has units of inverse length squared. This is a specialization with prescribed fields; the general problem allows any nonnegative $S\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$. The definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, a momentum constraint, or an asymptotically Euclidean or puncture solution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the domain $\Omega$ and exponent $\alpha$ of *Bounded-domain charged conformal problem*, let $X=\{u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$ and $Y=C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with the full norms specified there; the zero subscript denotes zero boundary restriction, not compact support. Then

$$-\Delta:X\longrightarrow Y$$

is a bounded linear isomorphism. Consequently $A:=-8\Delta:X\to Y$ is a bounded linear isomorphism and its inverse obeys $\|A^{-1}f\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\leq C(\Omega,\alpha)\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$.

Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, let $U\subset X\times\mathbb R$ be open in the max product norm, and let $F:U\to Y$ be continuously Fréchet differentiable. Assume $F(0,0)=0$ and that $L:=D_xF(0,0):X\to Y$ is a bounded linear isomorphism. Then there are $\rho,\epsilon_0>0$ and a unique $C^1$ map $x:(-\epsilon_0,\epsilon_0)\to B_X(0,\rho)$ such that $x(0)=0$ and $F(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)=0$; every zero in $B_X(0,\rho)\times(-\epsilon_0,\epsilon_0)$ lies on this graph. Its derivative is

$$x'(\epsilon)=-D_xF(x(\epsilon),\epsilon)^{-1}D_\epsilon F(x(\epsilon),\epsilon).$$

Let $X$ and $Y=C^{0,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ be the Hölder spaces with the norms specified in *Bounded-domain charged conformal problem*, and let $S\in Y$ be its source. The inclusion $X\hookrightarrow Y$ is bounded. The set $\mathcal U:=\{u\in Y:\min_{\overline\Omega}(1+u)>0\}$ is open, and

$$N_S:\mathcal U\to Y,\qquad N_S(u):=S(1+u)^{-3},$$

is continuously Fréchet differentiable with $DN_S(u)[h]=-3S(1+u)^{-4}h$ for every $u\in\mathcal U$ and $h\in Y$.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, nonempty and open. If $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C(\overline\Omega)$ and $\Delta u\ge0$, then
$$\max_{\overline\Omega}u=\max_{\partial\Omega}u.$$
No connectedness or boundary smoothness is required.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, $0<\alpha<1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty. Then $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with the norm of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] is a Banach space over $\mathbb K$: every Cauchy sequence in $\|\cdot\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ converges in that norm to a limit whose $k$-th partial derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder on $\Omega$. If in addition $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain with nonempty boundary, then the subspace
$$X_0:=\{u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega): u\text{ extends continuously to }\bar\Omega\text{ with }u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$$
is closed in $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega)$ and hence is a Banach space. For every bounded open nonempty $\Omega$, the boundary-extension class $C^{k,\alpha}(\bar\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is also a closed subspace of $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and hence a Banach space, as is its zero-boundary subspace. Completeness here is for the full finite Hölder norm. A boundary Hölder seminorm alone does not define a norm on this function space, since it vanishes on nonzero constant functions.

The set $U:=\{(u,\varepsilon)\in X\times\mathbb R:\min_{\overline\Omega}(1+u)>0\}$ is open because the minimum changes by at most $\|u-v\|_\infty$, which is bounded by the $X$-norm. Define $F:U\to Y$ by $F(u,\varepsilon):=Au-2\varepsilon^2N_S(u)$, with $A=-8\Delta$ and $N_S(u)=S(1+u)^{-3}$. By [A1], the inverse supplier [F2] applies; [F4] gives a continuously differentiable map on $Y$ and the bounded inclusion $X\hookrightarrow Y$, so $F$ is $C^1$. Also $F(0,0)=0$ and $D_uF(0,0)=A$, since the $u$-derivative of the nonlinear term is multiplied by $\varepsilon^2$.

Since $A$ is invertible, [F3] supplies $\rho,\varepsilon_0>0$ and a unique local $C^1$ branch $u_\varepsilon$ in the ball $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}<\rho$ satisfying $F(u_\varepsilon,\varepsilon)=0$. Shrink the product neighborhood so that $\|u_\varepsilon\|_\infty<1/2$; then $\psi_\varepsilon=1+u_\varepsilon>0$, and $F=0$ is equivalent to the defining Dirichlet equation.

For each $\varepsilon$, the equation and $S\geq0$ imply $\Delta u_\varepsilon\leq0$. Hence $\Delta(-u_\varepsilon)\geq0$ and $-u_\varepsilon=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. Applying [F5] to $-u_\varepsilon$ yields $\max_{\overline\Omega}(-u_\varepsilon)=0$, so $u_\varepsilon\geq0$ and $\psi_\varepsilon\geq1$.

Let $v:=A^{-1}(2S)$, which is the unique element of $X$ with $-8\Delta v=2S$. The fixed-point equation gives $u_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon^2A^{-1}\bigl(S(1+u_\varepsilon)^{-3}\bigr)$. If $S=0$, the same identity gives $u_\varepsilon=0$, so the zero-source case is included.

Subtract $A(\varepsilon^2v)=2\varepsilon^2S$ from $Au_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon^2S(1+u_\varepsilon)^{-3}$, obtaining $u_\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2v=2\varepsilon^2A^{-1}\!\left(S\bigl((1+u_\varepsilon)^{-3}-1\bigr)\right)$. The differentiability estimate in [F4] at $u=0$ gives $\|S((1+u_\varepsilon)^{-3}-1)\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}\leq C_1\|u_\varepsilon\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$ for small $\varepsilon$. Define $R(h)$ by $R^a{}_{bij}=\partial_{X^i}\Gamma(h)^a{}_{jb}-\partial_{X^j}\Gamma(h)^a{}_{ib}+\Gamma(h)^a{}_{ic}\Gamma(h)^c{}_{jb}-\Gamma(h)^a{}_{jc}\Gamma(h)^c{}_{ib}$, followed by the Ricci and scalar contractions of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Sobolev embedding gives $h\in C^{s-1}$ and $K,e,b\in C^{s-2}$; the uniform positive lower eigenvalue makes $h^{-1}$ well defined, and the smooth-composition and algebra suppliers give $\Gamma(h)\in H^s$, $R(h)\in H^{s-1}$, and $D K,D e,D b\in H^{s-1}$. Since $s\ge5$, these constraint terms have continuous representatives, and their displayed equalities mean pointwise equality of those representatives. In the SI interpretation, $K$ and $D$ carry one inverse-length factor, $R(h)$ and $\Lambda$ carry inverse-length squared, and the orthonormal components $e_A,b_A$ have units tesla; the factors $\kappa/\mu_0$ give matching units in the constraints. No numerical parameter values are assigned here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain and choose $R>0$ with $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^3$. Write $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of the compactly supported smooth functions. Then $\|v\|_{L^2}\le2R\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. A function $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ represents an element of $H^1_0(\Omega)$ if and only if $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: The base fields are smooth and $\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$, so the source in [F1] is the constant $S=a^2$, and scaling them by $\varepsilon$ preserves their zero divergences. The units are consistent: $a^2$ and $\Delta$ have units of inverse length squared, while $\psi$ and $\varepsilon$ are dimensionless.

Smoothness bootstrap, initial gain. Set $u=u_\varepsilon=\psi_\varepsilon-1$ and $f=(\varepsilon^2a^2/4)\psi_\varepsilon^{-3}$, so $-\Delta u=f$ and $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. The branch gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ and $\psi_\varepsilon\ge1$. The identities $\partial_i(\psi^{-3})=-3\psi^{-4}\partial_i\psi$ and $\partial_{ij}(\psi^{-3})=12\psi^{-5}(\partial_i\psi)(\partial_j\psi)-3\psi^{-4}\partial_{ij}\psi$ follow from [F11] and the product rule and show that $f\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, with bounded derivatives through order two, hence $f\in H^2(\Omega)$ by integration by parts against compactly supported tests. By [F6], $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Its classical equation tested against $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ gives the weak identity; continuity of both sides in the $H^1$ test norm and the defining density of $C_c^\infty$ in $H^1_0$ extend it to every test in $H^1_0$. Applying [F8] with $m=2$ yields $u\in H^4(\Omega)$.

On $B_R(0)$, define $v(x):=\frac{a^2}{24}(R^2-|x|^2)$. It vanishes on $\partial B_R$, and $\Delta |x|^2=6$ in $\mathbb R^3$, so $-8\Delta v=-8(-6a^2/24)=2a^2=2S$. By uniqueness of the zero-boundary solution in [F2], this is the coefficient in the branch expansion.

Smoothness bootstrap, composition and iteration. Fix an integer $m\ge4$ and suppose $\psi=1+u\in H^m(\Omega)$. Its continuous range is a compact interval $J\subset[1,\infty)$ by [F2] and [F9]. To verify $\psi^{-3}\in H^m$, use [F10] to choose smooth restrictions $\psi_n\to\psi$ in $H^m$; [F9] gives uniform convergence, so for all sufficiently large $n$ the values of $\psi_n$ lie in one compact interval $J'\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $J$. For each smooth $q$ with values in $J'$, repeated application of the total chain and product rules [F11] expresses every $D^\beta(q^{-3})$, $|\beta|\le m$, as a finite sum of bounded factors $G^{(r)}(q)$, $G(s)=s^{-3}$, times products $\prod_jD^{\gamma_j}q$ with $|\gamma_j|\ge1$ and $\sum_j|\gamma_j|=|\beta|$. Each product is in $L^2$ with a bound controlled by $\|q\|_{H^m}$: derivatives of order at most $m-2$ lie in $H^2$ or a higher Sobolev space and hence in $L^\infty$ by [F9]; a factor of order $m$ can occur only alone and is in $L^2$; a factor of order $m-1$ occurs at most once, lies in $H^1\subset L^6$, and any remaining factor has total derivative order at most one and lies in $L^\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto G'(q)$ is uniformly bounded in $H^m$ on the bounded smooth approximants and their line segments. The same difference identity applied to $G'$ shows $t\mapsto G'(\psi_\ell+t(\psi_n-\psi_\ell))$ is continuous in $H^m$, so its displayed integral exists as a Banach-valued Riemann integral. The identity $G(\psi_n)-G(\psi_\ell)=(\psi_n-\psi_\ell)\int_0^1G'(\psi_\ell+t(\psi_n-\psi_\ell))\,dt$, together with the Banach-algebra bound [F9], shows $G(\psi_n)$ is Cauchy in $H^m$. Its uniform limit is $G(\psi)$, proving $\psi^{-3}\in H^m$. Hence $f\in H^m$; [F8] gives $u\in H^{m+2}$. Starting with $m=4$ and repeating for $m=4,6,8,\ldots$ proves $u\in H^{2j}(\Omega)$ for every sufficiently large integer $j$. The same embeddings imply $u\in H^r(\Omega)$ for every finite integer $r$, and then $u\in C^k(\overline\Omega)$ for every $k$, so $\psi_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$.

Verification of the full constraints. On the oriented manifold without boundary $\Sigma=\Omega$, take the conformal seed data $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, $\Lambda=0$, $\bar E=\varepsilon a e_1$, and $\bar B=0$. Smoothness and positivity of $\psi_\varepsilon$ follow from steps 1.2–2.2 and [F2], so [F3] defines smooth $h,K,E,B$ and gives $K=0$. The Maxwell constraints hold because $\partial_i\bar E^i=\partial_i\bar B^i=0$ by step 1.1 and the barred metric is Euclidean. Since $\bar R=0$ and $|\bar E|_\delta^2=\varepsilon^2a^2$, the transformed Hamiltonian constraint [F4] is exactly $-8\Delta\psi_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon^2a^2\psi_\varepsilon^{-3}$, the branch equation. Its transformed momentum equation has zero left side because $K=\tau=0$ and zero right side because $\bar E\times_\delta\bar B=0$. Thus all four constraints in [F5] hold. The data are smooth constrained time-symmetric data on this fixed ball; the Dirichlet boundary value is prescribed, and the proof makes no claim of an isolated asymptotically flat black hole or any other boundary-value problem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

norm values are supplied by

for real scalars and

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying

Here the weak derivative is the one in

invariance under null-set changes follow from

Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
