The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. With $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|>0$ in the published chart/polar convention, set $\Phi(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $\Phi(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|$ for $n=2$, $x\ne0$. Extend it as a locally integrable function at the pole. The one-dimensional analogue is $-\tfrac12|x|$; the subsequent $n\ge2$ Green theory does not silently include it.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported
$f$, define
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$
at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral
is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class.
The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data
and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself
makes no unconditional convergence claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on

that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

supported, meaning that it has a representative which vanishes outside a
compact set. Then $Nf$ is finite almost everywhere, belongs to
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, and depends only on the $L^1$ equivalence
class of $f$. Its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n).$$

$1\le p\le\infty$. If $f=0$ almost everywhere outside a closed compact set
$K$, then $Nf$ is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^n\setminus K$.

The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

The remaining part is $(g(x')-g(x))\int_{B_M(m)\setminus B_d(m)}K_{ij}(x'-y)\,dy$. This kernel integral is bounded uniformly: the divergence theorem expresses it as the difference of two $D_i\Phi$ boundary fluxes; each sphere stays at least half its radius from the pole and has area proportional to its radius squared. The boundary correction from step 3.1 is also at most $C[g]_\alpha d^\alpha$. Hence $[D^2Ng]_{\alpha}\le C_\alpha[g]_\alpha$ on the box. The convergent far radial integral uses $\alpha<1$.

For $x\in B_1$, the support is in $B_3(x)$. Integrating $|\Phi|$ and $|D\Phi|$ over that ball bounds $|Ng|$ and $|DNg|$ by $C\|g\|_\infty$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume Countable Choice and fix $0<\alpha<1$. Put $B_R^+=B_R(0)\cap\{x_3>0\}$ and $T_R=B_R(0)\cap\{x_3=0\}$. For any nonempty set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with at least two points and any scalar or finite-dimensional array-valued $q$ on $A$, define $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=\sup_{x,y\in A,\,x\ne y}|q(x)-q(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, set $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=0$ when $A$ has at most one point, and define $\|q\|_{\infty;A}:=\sup_A|q|$, using the Euclidean norm for arrays. For a function $f$ on the closed half-ball, $C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_R^+})$ consists of continuous functions there with finite seminorm and norm $\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_R^+})}:=\|f\|_{\infty;\overline{B_R^+}}+[f]_{\alpha;\overline{B_R^+}}$; in this statement $[f]_\alpha$ and $\|f\|_\infty$ denote $[f]_{\alpha;\overline{B_R^+}}$ and $\|f\|_{\infty;\overline{B_R^+}}$. Suppose $u$ is bounded and has continuous partial derivatives through order $2$ in $B_R^+$ which extend continuously to every compact subset of $B_R\cap\{x_3\ge0\}$, $\Delta u=f$ in $B_R^+$, $u=0$ on $T_R$, and $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_R^+})$. There is no condition on the curved boundary and no requirement that $f|_{T_R}=0$. Then

$$\sum_{j=0}^2R^j\|D^ju\|_{\infty;B_{R/2}^+}+R^{2+\alpha}[D^2u]_{\alpha;B_{R/2}^+}\le C_\alpha\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R^+}+R^2\|f\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_\alpha\bigr).$$

The derivatives extend Hölder continuously to the flat face. The constant is independent of $R$ and of any higher derivative of a smooth approximant.

Assume Countable Choice. For a set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with at least two points, write $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=\sup_{x,y\in A,\,x\ne y}|q(x)-q(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, using absolute value for scalar $q$ and Euclidean array norm for finite-dimensional vector- or tensor-valued $q$; set $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=0$ when $A$ has at most one point. For nonempty $A$, put $\|q\|_{\infty;A}:=\sup_A|q|$. Globally $\alpha$-Hölder means continuous on $\mathbb R^3$ with $[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}<\infty$; set $[g]_\alpha:=[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}$, $\|g\|_\infty:=\|g\|_{\infty;\mathbb R^3}$, and $\|g\|_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^3}:=\|g\|_{\infty;\mathbb R^3}+[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}$. For an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $C^{2,\alpha}(V)$ means that the function has continuous partial derivatives through order $2$ on $V$ and $[D^2q]_{\alpha;K}<\infty$ for every compact $K\subset V$; $C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ means this property on every such $V$. In derivative-array norms below, $|D^jq|$ is the Euclidean norm of the array of order-$j$ partial derivatives and $\|D^jq\|_{\infty;B_R}:=\sup_{B_R}|D^jq|$. Let $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, and let $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be globally $\alpha$-Hölder with support in $B_{2R}(0)$. Put $Ng(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy$. Then $Ng\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Ng=g$, and

$$\sum_{j=0}^2R^j\|D^jNg\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^{2+\alpha}[D^2Ng]_{\alpha;B_R}\le C_\alpha R^2\bigl(\|g\|_\infty+R^\alpha[g]_\alpha\bigr).$$

The estimate uses the displayed scaled norms and is uniform in $R$ and $g$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

derivations.claim: Finite normalized charts. Near each boundary point rotate and translate so that the domain is $x_3>\varphi(x')$, with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $D\varphi(0)=0$. The shear $\Psi(y',t)=(y',t+\varphi(y'))$ maps the actual upper half-patch onto the domain portion of its image, and maps $t=0$ onto the boundary. Its inverse subtracts $\varphi$, its Jacobian determinant is one, and $J=D\Psi$ and $J^{-1}$ are bounded on smaller compact patches. Compactness of the smooth boundary permits a finite initial atlas. Further recenterings at nearby boundary points and rotations to their tangent planes have uniformly bounded derivatives on a common smaller radius: in each initial compact graph patch the normal derivative is bounded away from zero and the graph derivatives are bounded; solving the graph identity and differentiating gives these uniform bounds. Thus arbitrarily small radii $r$ can be used with one fixed bound on the first three chart derivatives, independent of the number of recentered patches.

For $v=u\circ\Psi$, the chain rule gives $D_yv=J^TD_xu$ and $D_y^2v=J^TD_x^2uJ+\sum_k u_{x_k}D_y^2\Psi_k$. Solving these identities expresses $\Delta_xu\circ\Psi=a^{ij}D_{ij}v+b^iD_iv$, with $a=J^{-1}J^{-T}$, $a(0)=I$, and bounded smooth $b$. On a radius-$r$ patch, $\|a-I\|_\infty\le C r$, while $[a]_\alpha$, $\|b\|_\infty$ and $[b]_\alpha$ are bounded uniformly for $r$ below the fixed atlas radius. Chain/product differences also give two-sided control of the local $C^{2,\alpha}$ norms. In particular the coefficient of the top-order seminorm in this comparison stays bounded as $r\downarrow0$; terms involving derivatives of charts and derivatives of $u$ of order at most two contribute a fixed-radius multiple of $\|u\|_{C^2}$. This follows from $[pq]_\alpha\le\|p\|_\infty[q]_\alpha+[p]_\alpha\|q\|_\infty$ and $[p\circ\Psi]_\alpha\le[p]_\alpha\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi)^\alpha$.

Local freezing. Write $f=\Delta u$. In a boundary half-patch, $\Delta_yv=f\circ\Psi+(I-a):D^2v-b\cdot Dv$ and $v=0$ on the flat face. Apply [F2], with outer radius $r$ and inner radius $r/2$. The seminorm part of the principal error is bounded by $C r[D^2v]_\alpha+C_r\|v\|_{C^2}$; its supremum contributes only $C_r\|v\|_{C^2}$ after rescaling. The drift product and its seminorm contribute only $C_r\|v\|_{C^2}$ because $Dv$ is Lipschitz on the convex half-ball. It follows, after the chart comparison in step 2.1, that $[D^2u]_{\alpha;\mathrm{inner\ patch}}\le C_0 r[D^2u]_{\alpha;\Omega}+C_r(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^2})$, where $C_0$ is independent of small $r$. For an interior ball, extend a cutoff times $f$ by zero, subtract its Newtonian potential, and bound the harmonic remainder by the averaging-kernel argument in [F3]. This gives the same bound without the $C_0r$ term. No regularity of a weak solution has been assumed in this use of a priori estimates.

Global seminorm absorption. At a fixed sufficiently small $r$, take boundary centers forming an $r$-net in the compact boundary and interior balls of comparable radii for points farther from the boundary. Use outer patches with fixed larger radii proportional to $r$ and controlled inner patches of radius proportional to $r$; the uniform bi-Lipschitz chart bounds of step 1.1 ensure that each point has a controlled inner patch containing its intersection with a Euclidean ball of radius $c r$, with $c>0$ independent of the number of centers. Compactness selects finitely many. A pair at distance below $c r$ is therefore in one controlled patch; a pair farther apart has Hessian difference quotient at most $2(c r)^{-\alpha}\|D^2u\|_\infty$. Taking a maximum of the local estimates, not a sum over patches, yields $[D^2u]_{\alpha;\Omega}\le C_1r[D^2u]_{\alpha;\Omega}+C_r(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^2})$. Choose $r$ with $C_1r<1/2$ and absorb. Thus $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le C(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^2})$, with the radius now fixed solely by the domain and exponent.

Removing the lower derivative terms. If the stated estimate were false, normalize zero-boundary $C^{2,\alpha}$ functions to obtain $\|u_j\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}=1$ and $\|\Delta u_j\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u_j\|_\infty\to0$. The finite chart atlas makes the function and gradient fields uniformly equicontinuous from their bounded next derivatives; the Hessians are equicontinuous from their common Hölder bound. Apply [F4] to this finite list of derivative fields. A subsequence converges uniformly on $\overline\Omega$; integration on coordinate segments in interior balls identifies its derivative fields. Since $u_j\to0$ uniformly, its first and second derivative limits vanish in the interior and, by continuity, on the closure. Thus $\|u_j\|_{C^2}\to0$. Step 4.1 then gives $1\le C(\|\Delta u_j\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u_j\|_{C^2})\to0$, a contradiction. This proves the full a priori estimate with only the supremum of $u$ on the right.

All charts, radii and constants were fixed by $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ before the solution was chosen. Reflection and the Newtonian kernel enter through [F2], flattening and coefficient perturbation were derived in steps 1.1--3.1, and the finite-cover and compactness arguments in steps 4.1--5.1 complete the claimed global estimate. No published boundary or global Schauder theorem is an input.
